title: A contact path for a developer-tool company
metaTitle: A contact path for a developer-tool company
excerpt: Tell an engineer what happens after they write, how soon, and what to have ready. Point everyone else back to trying the product. A ten-field form loses the thread.
alt: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table. The article is about making a human reply as clear as the work on the table.
caption: A contact path should be as concrete as the notes already on the table. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Who should use a developer-tool contact form?
faqs.answer: Use it for a security review, a contract, or a problem the docs and the trial did not answer. Bugs belong in the issue tracker. Candidates belong on the careers page. The top of the page should point everyone else at the try path.

faqs.question: What should the page say about response time?
faqs.answer: Say who replies and how soon, in a sentence you will keep, such as a person on the next business day or a calendar invite that is itself the reply. Do not promise an instant answer you have not staffed. Repeat the same sentence in the confirmation.

faqs.question: Which form fields are worth requiring?
faqs.answer: Require a reply address and the question. Add a topic only if it changes who reads the note. Phone numbers, employee counts, and budget fields serve a forecast, not the first reply, so make them optional or remove them.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A developer-tool company contact page should tell an engineer who is skeptical of marketing what happens after they reach out, how soon a person replies, and what to have ready. The action on the rest of the site is to try the product. This page should not undo that. A form with ten fields is a way to lose someone who was willing to talk after they had already seen the tool work.

Write the page as a small, true promise. Who will read the note. What they will do next. What the reader can do instead, which is usually to try the product or open the docs. The companies that earn trust here sound like their README. The ones that lose it sound like a lead form with a friendlier font.

## The action is still to try

Open by pointing at the try path, in the same words as the homepage. Sandbox, install, or quickstart. Many engineers land on a contact page because a menu called contact was the only verb they recognized, or because they are stuck. Give them the exit back to the tool before you ask them to write.

Then say who should use the form. A security review. A contract above the published price. A bug you could not reproduce from the docs. Everyone else should be routed. Customers go to the issue tracker or the support address in the product. Job seekers go to careers. The form stays for the cases a trial cannot finish.

Put that sorting in the first screen. People decide quickly whether a page is worth the trouble. Nielsen Norman Group's research summary says users often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 seconds are the judgment. A wall of empty fields with no routing spends the judgment on clerical work. Lead with where to go. Offer the form to the people who remain.

If you embed a scheduler, say what the meeting is. "Twenty minutes on a migration you have already tried." That sentence filters the curious and prepares the serious. "Let's hop on a call" prepares no one. This reader does not want to hop. They want an agenda.

## What happens after they send it

Describe the next hour or the next business day in a sentence you will keep. "A person who works on the tool replies within one business day." Or "You will pick a time, and the invite is the reply." Choose one. Write it above the form. Repeat it in the confirmation.

Do not promise instant response unless a human actually does that. Engineers test promises the way they test timeouts. A missed instant reply becomes a story. A kept one-day reply becomes a reason to trust the changelog too. Staff the sentence you print.

Say what the reply will contain. A question, a link to a doc you should have found, or a proposed time. Say what it will not contain. A drip of nurture emails. A surprise calendar hold. If your process includes a sequence, admit it and give them a way to decline. Hidden sequences are how a contact page becomes spam, and this audience has a short block list.

Tell them how to know it worked. A confirmation on the page and a note in their inbox. If you send nothing, say that a lack of error means you have it, and still send something. Silence after a submit feels like a dropped packet. They will retry, or they will leave, and you will have two half-threads or none.

Keep the promise identical to any "talk to us" label in the header. If one path says security review and another says a specialist will reach out soon, you have two policies. Publish one.

## What to have ready

Ask for the material that makes a reply useful, and keep the form shorter than the prose. In the prose, suggest a reproduction. The version. The command. What they expected. What the tool did. A repo you are allowed to see, or a reduced sample. That is the shape of a good issue, and a good contact note looks like one.

On the form itself, require less. A reply address. A short textarea. A choice of topic if routing truly changes the recipient. Security, contract, product. Three topics, not thirty. If you do not route, skip the dropdown.

Tell them what not to prepare. A slide deck. A guess at your internal architecture. A legal review before anyone has confirmed the tool fits. The try path is the preparation for most product questions. Say that. "If you have not run the sample, start there. If you have, send the output."

A file upload can exist for a log, with a size limit stated. It should be optional. Many readers will paste the relevant lines. Forcing an attachment is a reason to postpone, and postponing on a contact page usually means not coming back.

## Why a long form confirms their skepticism

Each extra field looks innocent in a spreadsheet of lead quality. Together they say you care more about the record than the question. Title, phone, employee count, budget, how they heard about you, a required checkbox novella. The engineer came with a failing build or a procurement gate. You handed them intake.

Cut to the reply address and the question. If sales needs a phone number, make it optional and say why. "Only if the meeting link fails." A required mobile number will be filled with zeros or will end the visit. Neither helps the call.

Employee count and budget rarely change the first reply. They change a forecast. Collect them later, from a conversation the person chose. A required range with no honest bucket teaches them that the form is for you. Google's people-first content guidance applies to this page as a task. Help them finish the task they arrived with. The task is to reach the right human or to get back to the tool. Enriching a profile is not their task.

Dropdowns that do not include the true category are a special irritation. If the honest answer is "none of these," delete the field. Do not offer "other" as a confession.

## Make the remaining path obvious

Label the submit button with the result. "Send to the maintainers." "Request a security review." "Book a migration review." Avoid "Submit." Avoid "Let's go." The button should sound like the promise at the top of the page.

Afterward, confirm the same promise. "A maintainer will reply by the next business day. If you are blocked now, the docs cover the install and the sandbox." The confirmation is part of the page. A generic thank-you is a missed chance to point them at the try path one more time, in case the form was the wrong door.

Publish one email address as well, for the reader who will not use a form. Put it in text, not in an image. Say which mail it is. Security and general product mail can be different addresses if you actually read them separately. One mailbox that you read is better than four you do not. State the same response window.

Do not cover the form with a chat bubble. A second voice asking if they need help, while they are writing to you, is noise. If chat is for customers inside the product, keep it there. The public contact page should be calm enough to paste a stack trace.

## Route everyone else in one line

Give the wrong visitors a correct door. Bugs go to the issue tracker, with the template linked. Customers go to the in-product support. Candidates go to roles. Each route is a sentence and a link. No scolding. A person who mis-clicked should be gone in a tap, and the people who belong should find a quieter form because of it.

If you are the wrong tool, say so. "If you need a hosted data warehouse, this is not one." The engineer who fits will trust the fence. The engineer who does not will save both of you the thread. A contact page that accepts every kind of hope will spend its week saying no slowly. Saying no on the page is faster and kinder.

Keep the tone free of the slogan you avoided on the homepage. This is not the place to empower anyone. It is the place to answer, route, or invite a trial. Plain sentences will feel like the product if the product is plain. If the product is not plain, the contact page is a poor place to invent a new voice.

## Check it the way they will

Open the page on a phone. Read the first screen. Can you tell whether to try the tool, file an issue, or write? Complete the form with a thumb. If the textarea is short and the page jumps when the keyboard opens, fix the layout. Reserve space. Make the confirmation visible without a hunt.

Send a note to yourself through the real path. Measure it against the sentence on the page. Did a person reply in the window? Did the reply answer the question, or did it ask you to book a different call and fill a different tool? Align the hour with the sentence. The page is a spec for the inbox. When the inbox drifts, update one of them the same day.

Then remove one field. The field you added to be safe is the one to test. Required fields should change the route or the reply. Everything else can be optional prose in the textarea, where a reader who cares will put it, and a reader in a hurry will not be stopped.

The contact page collects habits the rest of the site should have lost. A slogan, a long form, a vague promise of partnership. Read [what to take off the site for this buyer](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-developer-tool-company) and apply the same cut here. The form should get shorter, not warmer.

When you want the promise and the form checked together, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the fields and the sentence about what happens next. The mismatch is the brief.
